title: “Before the angel” — the Greek has “in the presence of God”
summary: The KJV places the excuse that something was an error before the angel. The old Greek translation places it before God.
text: KJV Ecclesiastes 5:6: “Suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin; neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error: wherefore should God be angry at thy voice, and destroy the work of thine hands?” Hebrew text 5:5: אַל־תִּתֵּ֤ן אֶת־פִּ֙יךָ֙ לַחֲטִ֣יא אֶת־בְּשָׂרֶ֔ךָ וְאַל־תֹּאמַר֙ לִפְנֵ֣י הַמַּלְאָ֔ךְ כִּ֥י שְׁגָגָ֖ה הִ֑יא לָ֣מָּה יִקְצֹ֤ף הָֽאֱלֹהִים֙ עַל־קֹולֶ֔ךָ וְחִבֵּ֖ל אֶת־מַעֲשֵׂ֥ה יָדֶֽיךָ׃ Old Greek translation 5:5: Μὴ δῷς τὸ στόμα σου τοῦ ἐξαμαρτῆσαι τὴν σάρκα σου, καὶ μὴ εἴπῃς πρὸ προσώπου τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὅτι ἄγνοιά ἐστιν· ἵνα μὴ ὀργισθῇ ὁ Θεὸς ἐπὶ φωνῇ σου, καὶ διαφθείρῃ τὰ ποιήματα χειρῶν σου. The English version of the old Greek translation (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/ECC05.htm) prints: “Suffer not thy mouth to lead thy flesh to sin; and say not in the presence of God, It was an error: lest God be angry at thy voice, and destroy the works of thy hands.”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/21/5/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ECC05.htm.
reasoning: Both texts warn against letting speech lead to sin and offering an excuse. They differ in the named hearer: angel or messenger in the KJV, God in the Greek.
scope: The comparison is KJV Ecclesiastes 5:6 beside printed Hebrew and Greek 5:5. Only the angel/God clause is compared; the verse numbers must remain distinct. The English version of the old Greek translation (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/ECC05.htm) prints: “For he shall not much remember the days of his life; for God troubles him in the mirth of his heart.”. title: “Nor known any thing” — the Greek has the unborn child not knowing “rest”
summary: At Ecclesiastes 6:5, the KJV says the unborn child has not seen the sun or known anything. The old Greek translation says the child has not known rest.

Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/21/6/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ECC06.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew rest word follows the wording about not knowing. The KJV places rest in the next clause, while the Greek joins it to what is not known.
scope: Only the quoted clause at Ecclesiastes 6:5 is compared. This is not a general claim about awareness after death. title: “A thousand years twice told” — the Greek has no ‘twice’
summary: At Ecclesiastes 6:6, the KJV gives a thousand years twice told. The old Greek translation refers to returns of a thousand years without an explicit twice.

reasoning: The absence of twice is the finding. The Greek plural returns does not state a total of exactly one thousand years. It therefore does not establish totals differing by a factor of two.

title: “Withdraw not thine hand” — the Greek has “defile not thine hand”
summary: At Ecclesiastes 7:18, the KJV tells the reader not to withdraw the hand. The old Greek translation instead says not to defile the hand.
text: KJV Ecclesiastes 7:18: “It is good that thou shouldest take hold of this; yea, also from this withdraw not thine hand: for he that feareth God shall come forth of them all.” Hebrew text 7:18: טֹ֚וב אֲשֶׁ֣ר תֶּאֱחֹ֣ז בָּזֶ֔ה וְגַם־מִזֶּ֖ה אַל־תַּנַּ֣ח אֶת־יָדֶ֑ךָ כִּֽי־יְרֵ֥א אֱלֹהִ֖ים יֵצֵ֥א אֶת־כֻּלָּֽם׃ Old Greek translation 7:18: Ἀγαθὸν τὸ ἀντέχεσθαί σε ἐν τούτῳ, καί γε ἀπὸ τούτου μὴ μιάνῃς τὴν χεῖρά σου, ὅτι φοβουμένοις τὸν Θεὸν ἐξελεύσεται τὰ πάντα. The English version of the old Greek translation (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/ECC07.htm) prints: “It is well for thee to hold fast by this; also by this defile not thine hand: for to them that fear God all things shall come forth well.”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/21/7/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ECC07.htm.
reasoning: Both texts first describe taking hold of this and that. The following command differs: keep holding on or avoid defiling the hand.

title: “And in the sight of thine eyes” — the Greek adds “blameless” and a negative
summary: At Ecclesiastes 11:9, the KJV tells the young man to walk by his heart and what his eyes see. The old Greek translation adds blameless and not before the phrase about his eyes.
text: KJV Ecclesiastes 11:9: “Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thine heart, and in the sight of thine eyes: but know thou, that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment.” Hebrew text 11:9: שְׂמַ֧ח בָּח֣וּר בְּיַלְדוּתֶ֗יךָ וִֽיטִֽיבְךָ֤ לִבְּךָ֙ בִּימֵ֣י בְחוּרֹותֶ֔ךָ וְהַלֵּךְ֙ בְּדַרְכֵ֣י לִבְּךָ֔ וּבְמַרְאֵ֖י עֵינֶ֑יךָ וְדָ֕ע כִּ֧י עַל־כָּל־אֵ֛לֶּה יְבִֽיאֲךָ֥ הָאֱלֹהִ֖ים בַּמִּשְׁפָּֽט׃ Old Greek translation 11:9: Εὐφραίνου νεανίσκε ἐν νεότητί σου, καὶ ἀγαθυνάτω σε ἡ καρδία σου ἐν ἡμέραις νεότητός σου, καὶ περιπάτει ἐν ὁδοῖς καρδίας σου ἄμωμος, καὶ μὴ ἐν ὁράσει ὀφθαλμῶν σου· καὶ γνῶθι ὅτι ἐπὶ πᾶσι τούτοις ἄξει σε ὁ Θεὸς ἐν κρίσει. The English version of the old Greek translation (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/ECC11.htm) prints: “Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thy heart blameless, but not in the sight of thine eyes: yet know that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment.”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/21/11/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ECC11.htm.
reasoning: The added negative reverses that clause about the eyes, and blameless further qualifies the instruction. Both versions keep the closing warning about judgment.

title: “Childhood and youth are vanity” — the Greek has “youth and folly”
summary: At Ecclesiastes 11:10, the KJV calls childhood and youth vanity. The old Greek translation instead names youth and folly.

The English version of the old Greek translation (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/ECC11.htm) prints: “Therefore remove sorrow from thy heart, and put away evil from thy flesh: for youth and folly are vanity.”.
